evidence_quotes.quote: Rural village community use of this grey-water in permaculture projects to irrigate borehole gardens is proposed to primarily provide economic benefit whereby garden-produce revenue helps fund borehole water-point maintenance.
Stakeholder interviews in 2012-13 (Halcrow, 2013) to identify confounding technical, economic, social and governance issues that impinge upon permaculture performance

This initiative included training of communities and other stakeholders on IWRM and primarily aimed to introduce borehole-garden permaculture as a key opportunity. Training was provided on the technical development of income-generating gardens, including life-cycle costing.

Malawian government guidelines stipulate all community-based operations and management should be voluntary and unpaid; community-based management is a cornerstone of rural Malawi. Hence all work on WPCs, overarching Water Users Association (WUA) and permaculture-garden related activities is voluntary.

A high proportion (98%) of boreholes was functional with 72% having routine servicing. Communities had designed their tariff structure based upon full-cost recovery with support from government workers that had allowed inclusion of permaculture garden accounting and water-point banking in a transparent manner.

Permaculture implementations total 123 representing 6% of the mapped water points. Uptake is predominantly along the Mwanza Valley, especially in TA Chapananga where permaculture is employed at 26% of the 412 water points mapped

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural village hand-pump boreholes (water points) supplying domestic and drinking water in Chikwawa District, Malawi, focusing on borehole-garden permaculture (reusing spilt hand-pump grey-water) as a mechanism to generate revenue for water-point maintenance and sustain community water supply alongside food security and stagnant-pond malaria control.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 but FAILS the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading. Under the plain wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper examines local institutional and community-governance arrangements—including Water Point Committees (WPCs), Water Users Associations, village chiefs, NGO-ministry coordination via the District Executive Committee/District Co-ordinating Team, voluntary community-based management norms, and NGO IWRM promotion (which supported WPC formation, full-cost-recovery tariff calculation, and water-point banking)—so plain_criterion2_decision is 'include' (albeit borderline because most governance analysis focuses on permaculture garden uptake and abandonment rather than water access). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, c2 is 'no': the study evaluates an agro-ecological grey-water gardening practice ('borehole-garden permaculture') and generic NGO/multi-sector IWRM promotion, technical training, and institutional coordination, rather than empirically analysing a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access or disconnection, or regulatory structure). Mentions of full-cost-recovery tariffs, voluntary unpaid WPC/garden labour, and 2013 gravel-bed soakaway drainage rules are descriptive context or concern incentives to maintain vegetable gardens rather than rules governing water access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence from Chikwawa District (2012-14 semi-structured stakeholder interviews across nine stakeholder groups; 2013 Health Surveillance Assistant survey of stagnant ponds across 1,894 mapped water points; 2015 questionnaire survey evaluating IWRM promotion in 18 villages; 2015-16 FLOW asset-register mapping of 2,067 water points; and June 2017 field visits to 65 villages / 33 gardens), alongside financial scoping estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Although the primary outcomes are borehole-garden permaculture uptake (123 of 2,067 water points), stagnant-pond prevalence (388 of 1,894 water points), and garden crop profitability, the paper also reports secondary descriptive and qualitative water-service outcomes: borehole functionality (98% functional and 72% with routine servicing in the 18 promoted villages), less problematic tariff collection, qualitative stakeholder reports of rapid repair of malfunctioning boreholes, and daily water-point abstraction/spillage (~5,000 l/d for ~80 households).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (rural communities and hand-pump water points in Chikwawa District, Malawi), exposure (borehole-garden permaculture implementation and NGO/multi-sector IWRM promotional/training activities), outcomes (permaculture uptake/profitability, stagnant pond occurrence, and descriptive borehole functionality/maintenance), and study design (mixed-methods observational case study and implementation evaluation) are identifiable.

study_design: Mixed-methods observational case study and implementation evaluation (semi-structured stakeholder interviews, cross-sectional water-point and stagnant-pond mapping surveys, post-promotion village questionnaire survey, field site visits, and scoping financial analysis)
population_and_sample: Rural village communities and community hand-pump boreholes (water points) in Chikwawa District, Southern Malawi: stakeholder interviews across 9 groups (2013); 1,894 water points surveyed for stagnant ponds (2013); questionnaire survey across 18 villages / 57 water-point banks in Chapananga TA (2015); 2,067 mapped water points across Chikwawa (2015-16); and field visits to 65 villages / 33 borehole gardens in Kakoma (2017).
exposure: Borehole-garden permaculture implementation (irrigating small community vegetable gardens with spilt hand-pump grey-water) and NGO/multi-sector IWRM promotional, training, and community-management support activities
outcome: Primary: permaculture garden uptake (6% of 2,067 District water points), stagnant-pond prevalence (20.5% of 1,894 water points), garden success/failure factors, crop revenue, and water-point bank savings ($8,035 across 57 banks). Secondary water-supply outcomes: descriptive borehole functionality (98% functional, 72% routine servicing in 18 promoted villages), qualitative reports of rapid borehole repair, and daily water abstraction/wastage.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. The study evaluates borehole-garden permaculture—an agro-ecological grey-water reuse intervention around rural hand-pump boreholes—together with NGO/multi-stakeholder IWRM promotion, agricultural/technical training, and district-community coordination. While the paper discusses institutional and governance arrangements (Water Point Committees, village chiefs, NGO-ministry coordination, voluntary garden labour norms, and bundled support for full-cost-recovery tariff accounting and water-point banking) and would pass a broad literal reading of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'), it does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community water service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure barriers, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access or disconnection, or utility regulatory structure).
